items.title: Flyers activate Rasmus Ristolainen off injured reserve
items.desc: Ristolainen has missed 16 total games with a hand injury this season.

stories.take:
Daily Faceoff reports the Flyers have activated defenseman Rasmus Ristolainen off injured reserve. He has missed 16 total games with a hand injury this season.

He comes back to a team that needs help. PHI sits at 5-10-5 and has had about 44% of the expected goals (a measure of shot quality) so far this season, so the underlying play matches the record. Ristolainen has played four games, scoring once from 0.33 expected goals, and he has been on the ice for only about 30% of the five-on-five expected goals while he's out there. That is a small sample, but it's a rough restart: the team has been 13 percentage points better with him off the ice. He was drafted eighth overall by the Sabres in 2013, and he logged more than 17 minutes a night in those four games. We'd watch whether that workload holds, because the Flyers don't have much room to ease anyone in.

items.desc: Kyle Davidson expressed support for coach Jeff Blashill amid a six-game losing streak. “I believe in Blash and his group,” Davidson said. “The players do, too. We’re aligned in that.”

stories.take:
The Athletic reports that Blackhawks GM Kyle Davidson is standing by coach Jeff Blashill during a six-game losing streak, saying "I believe in Blash and his group," and adds that Davidson is actively seeking trades.

Our numbers suggest the problem runs deeper than coaching or bad luck alone. Chicago is 4-13-1 and holds just 41.8% of the expected goals (a measure of chance quality) so far this season, so the team is being outplayed more often than not. At five-on-five that share is 41%. The results are worse than even that weak process: the Blackhawks have scored 8.7 fewer goals than expected, and their goaltending has saved 9.6 fewer goals than expected. The goalie-driven part of the gap means some of the pain is not purely the skaters, but a team that doesn't generate or suppress quality chances gives its goalies little help. The power play is generating 0.48 expected goals per game, which is modest. If Davidson does make a trade, we'd watch whether it addresses chance creation and goaltending, since both are dragging on this team right now.

items.desc: Ilya Safonov had only four assists in 12 AHL games with Vancouver’s minor-league affiliate, the Abbotsford Canucks.

stories.take:
Daily Faceoff reports that the Canucks placed Ilya Safonov on waivers to terminate his contract, noting he had only four assists in 12 AHL games with Abbotsford. It's a small move for a team in a deep hole.

Vancouver sits at 3-16-1 with 7 points through 20 games, and the numbers say the record is not an accident. The Canucks have generated just 39.9% of the expected goals (a measure of chance quality) so far this season, and 41% at five-on-five, so they are being outplayed in most of their games. Their goaltending has made it worse: goals saved above expected, which compares the goals a team's goalies allowed to what the shot quality predicts, sits at -14.8. Offsetting that, the skaters have scored 6.1 more goals than expected, which means the offense has been slightly lucky, not unlucky. Fixing the crease alone won't turn this around, because the underlying play is weak too. Removing a fringe prospect doesn't change any of that, but it does show a team trying to clear roster space while the real problems sit elsewhere.

stories.take: Daily Faceoff passes on Kevin Weekes' report that Matvei Michkov wants "a new start elsewhere," the loudest turn yet in a month of headlines about his ice time. Our numbers explain both sides. Michkov has 10 goals and 14 points in 20 games while playing 15.9 minutes a night, and seven of his points have come on the power play. He is also scoring well above his chances (4.5 goals more than expected), and at five on five the Flyers get just 40.5% of the expected goals (the quality of chances) with him on the ice. A coach can read that as a defensive problem; a player can read it as being buried on a team at 43.7% overall. Either way, the 2023 No. 7 pick is the rebuild's centerpiece, and this is now the Flyers' biggest story.

items.title: Report: Wild’s Brock Faber expected to make season debut Saturday
items.desc: Faber suffered a fractured skull and underwent surgery during the preseason and has been out of the lineup since September

stories.take:
Daily Faceoff reports that Minnesota's Brock Faber is expected to make his season debut Saturday. He suffered a fractured skull and underwent surgery during the preseason, and has been out of the lineup since September.

The Wild have not needed him to look good. They sit at 13-3-4 with 30 points through 20 games, and so far this season they have controlled 55.8 percent of the expected goals, which measures the quality of chances each side creates. At five-on-five that share is 53 percent, so the edge is real but modest. What stands out is the goaltending: the team is 14 goals better than expected in net, while its shooters are 8.3 goals worse than expected, meaning the finishing has trailed the chances. The special teams are solid too, generating 0.92 expected goals per game on the power play and allowing 0.7 per game on the penalty kill. Adding a healthy Faber to a group already winning without him is the kind of boost that can lift the underlying numbers further, and a return like this is worth watching on the ice.

stories.take: Daily Faceoff reports Nick Cousins left Tuesday's game after a hit from Jakob Chychrun, with no penalty called on the play. It came on an awkward night for Ottawa: the Senators had 70 shot attempts to Washington's 40 and by our replay deserved the game 63% of the time, then lost 3-2 in overtime. Losing Cousins for any stretch thins a forward group that has kept Ottawa at 11-6-2 with roughly even chances (52% of the expected goals, the quality of chances). The Senators' record has run a little behind their play this season, about three goals short on finishing. If Cousins misses time, watch who the coach moves up; depth scoring is where Ottawa has been leaving goals on the table.

stories.take: Daily Faceoff says the Bruins, first in the Atlantic at 13-4-1, are trending toward being cautious buyers. Cautious is the right word. Boston has controlled almost exactly half the play (50.6% of the expected goals, the quality of chances), and the record rests on two things that tend to fade: shooters 9.1 goals above their chances and goaltending that has saved 15.5 goals more than expected. That's a good team having a great month. Adding at the deadline makes sense if the target fixes the five-on-five gap rather than rewarding the hot start; a move made on the strength of the standings alone is how buyers end up disappointed in April.

items.title: 'Uncertainty With My Career': Hellebuyck Explains Factors Leading To Trade Request From Jets
items.desc: After months of speculation, a trade request, and a standoff between the Winnipeg Jets and Connor Hellebuyck, the 33-year-old attempted to clear the air on Tuesday in his return to the city he called home for the past 11 seasons.

stories.take:
Scott Arniel isn't pretending the Connor Hellebuyck trade was amicable. Asked by The Hockey News about New Jersey sitting Hellebuyck ahead of his return to Canada Life Centre, the Jets coach's answer made the headline: "He just gave up on us."

That is the story, and it will follow Hellebuyck into Winnipeg whenever he does play there. On the ice, the split so far is less dramatic than the words. In five games for the Devils he's at +1.46 goals saved above expected (saves beyond what the shot quality predicts), good but not carrying anyone, on a 13-5-0 team that takes 59% of the expected goals. Winnipeg is 7-8-3, has 48% of the chances and has scored 7.2 fewer goals than its looks usually produce. The Jets' hole is at the other end of the rink, which probably makes hearing about the goalie harder, not easier.

stories.take:
The Hockey News, citing Sportsnet's Elliotte Friedman, reports that Canadiens prospects Michael Hage and Alexander Zharovsky "will be available" to Montreal at the end of the season. In plain terms: when their current seasons finish, the Canadiens expect to be able to bring them in.

That's a good problem for an 11-3-3 team, but our numbers say the current group needs help more than the standings suggest. Montreal has 49% of the expected goals (the quality of chances) overall. The record leans on goaltending, which has saved 6.6 goals above expected. At five on five the share is a healthier 52%, so this isn't a mirage, but it's not a juggernaut either.

Prospects arriving in the spring rarely change a season. What it does is give Montreal options: in a playoff race, or a deep run, two skilled young forwards are a nice thing to have in reserve if the saves start to run out.

items.title: Rangers, James Reimer Contract Termination Echoes Historically Harsh Reality For Multiple Longtime NHL Goaltenders
items.desc: The New York Rangers have mutually agreed to terminate the contract of goalie James Reimer on Saturday. But while this is likely the end of Reimer's NHL career, his longevity is to be admired. Even the best goalies end their NHL careers in a non-ideal manner.

stories.take:
The Rangers and James Reimer have mutually agreed to terminate his contract, The Hockey News reports, and the outlet frames it as the likely end of his NHL career. It came a day after Daily Faceoff reported he had been placed on waivers.

The end was quiet on the ice too. Reimer appeared in one game this season, in relief, and allowed three goals on eight shots. Last season he played 14 games at 1.67 goals below expected. That is not how anyone in Toronto will remember him. A fourth-round pick of the Leafs in 2006, "Optimus Reim" became a cult favourite there before long stops across the league, and lasting as an NHL goalie for well over a decade is rare. As The Hockey News puts it, even the best goalies rarely get to leave on their own terms.

For New York, nothing changes in net. The Rangers' worry is finishing: 5.66 fewer goals than their chances usually produce.
